notes.meaning: The people wondered why God had not rescued them from their troubles. Isaiah answers that the Lord's hand has not lost its strength, nor is he too hard of hearing to catch their cries. The delay did not come from any lack of power in God.
The real barrier between God and the people was their own persistent sin. Their wrongful actions had built a wall of separation, causing God to turn his face away and refuse to hear their prayers.
The prophet names the specific evils that cut the people off from God. Their hands were stained with violence and unjust bloodshed, and their mouths were busy spreading lies and corrupt talk.

No one went to court to seek genuine justice or argue an honest case. Instead, people relied on empty excuses and false claims, constantly planning trouble in their minds and carrying out harm against others.
Wicked schemes are compared to poisonous snake eggs and fragile spider webs. Anyone who joins in these deadly plans meets ruin, and trying to break them open only releases more venomous harm.
A spider web can never be woven into clothes to keep anyone warm or covered. In the same way, human schemes and violent deeds can never hide a person's guilt or make them right before God.
The people were eager to do wrong, running swiftly to harm the innocent. Their minds were filled with destructive plans, leaving pain and devastation wherever they walked.
The people knew nothing of true peace with God, with other people, or in their own hearts. They chose crooked and dishonest paths, and anyone who follows those ways will never find lasting peace.

Isaiah begins a humble prayer of confession on behalf of the whole nation. Because the people refused to practice justice, God withheld his rescue, leaving them to search for light while stumbling in thick darkness.

The people felt helpless and confused, like blind travelers groping along a wall. Even at bright noontime they tripped as if it were dark night, wandering without hope or strength like people in the grave.

The community expressed its sorrow in two ways, growling like hungry bears in frustration and moaning softly like lonely doves. They kept hoping for rescue and justice, but their sins kept God's salvation far away.
The people openly admitted that their rebellious acts had piled up before God. Their sins stood like witnesses in court proving their guilt, leaving them unable to deny their wrongdoing.

The confession spells out how deeply they had turned away from the Lord through outright betrayal and deceit. They planned lies in their hearts and used their words to cheat and oppress their neighbors.
Justice and fairness were completely driven out of public life. Truth was pictured as falling down in the open city square, and honesty was locked outside the gates of the courtroom.

Honesty had vanished so completely that anyone trying to turn away from evil became an easy target for wicked people. The Lord saw this moral breakdown, and he was deeply displeased that no justice remained.

God saw that no human champion stepped forward to defend the truth or intercede, which means to stand in the gap and pray for help. Because no person could rescue the people, the Lord used his own mighty arm and his own righteousness to bring deliverance.

The Lord prepared for battle like a warrior putting on divine armor. He wore righteousness as a breastplate, placed salvation on his head like a helmet, and wrapped himself in holy zeal and judgment against evil.
God will give his enemies exactly what their deeds deserve. He will unleash righteous anger against his adversaries and bring fair judgment even to distant lands and islands across the sea.

People from the west to the rising sun in the east will honor and revere the Lord when they witness his power. His arrival to put down evil and deliver his people will rush in with the force of a mighty river driven by a powerful wind.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that the Hebrew describes the Lord Himself rushing in like a pent-up river driven by the wind, rather than an enemy coming like a flood and the Spirit raising a banner.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises that the Redeemer will come to Zion to set his people free. A redeemer was a family protector who bought back relatives from debt or slavery, and here God promises freedom to everyone who turns away from sin.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this prophecy points specifically to the end times, when ethnic Israel will recognize Jesus as the Messiah and be spiritually saved.
Reformed and Presbyterian Christians generally view Zion as the Christian church, seeing this promise fulfilled through Christ's first coming and the gospel calling all believers to repent.

notes.meaning: God confirms his covenant, his solemn promise and lasting agreement, with his redeemed people. He promises that his Holy Spirit and the words of truth he gave them will never leave them, their children, or future generations.
